Every route built so far. Start: db, redis, ollama, `make migrate`, `make dev`, `make worker`. Then Run collection on folders 0 to 6. Folder 7 is manual.

Write routes allow 10 requests per minute per user per route; a full run stays under that. Running it twice within a minute can hit 429 on sign-up (limited by IP): wait a minute.

{
  "title": "Billing guide",
  "body": "Acme Billing is the payments product used by all paid workspaces. This guide answers the questions support gets most often.

# Plans and pricing

Acme has three plans: Free, Team, and Business. Prices are per seat, billed monthly or yearly.

Yearly billing gives two months free. Switching from monthly to yearly takes effect at the next renewal date.

## Changing plans

Upgrades apply immediately and the customer is charged a prorated amount for the rest of the billing period.

Downgrades apply at the end of the current period. Features from the higher plan stay active until then.

# Refunds

## Full refunds

Customers can get a full refund within 14 days of their first payment. After 14 days, only partial refunds are possible.

To issue a full refund, open the invoice in the admin panel and click Refund. The money returns to the original card in 5 to 10 business days.

## Partial refunds

Partial refunds cover unused seats only. They are calculated per day from the date the seat was removed until the end of the billing period. Agents must not promise a partial refund for a downgrade, because downgrades take effect at the end of the period and nothing is unused. If a customer was charged twice for the same invoice, that is not a partial refund case: escalate it to the payments team with the two charge ids, since duplicate charges usually mean a webhook retried and the fix has to happen on the payment provider side as well. Refunds over 500 USD need approval from a team lead before they are issued, and the approval must be noted on the ticket. Refunds can never be sent to a different card than the one that was charged, even if the original card has expired; the bank forwards the money to the replacement card automatically.

# Failed payments

When a card payment fails, Acme retries it after 1, 3, and 7 days. After the third failure the workspace is moved to read-only mode.

To check a failed payment from the command line:

```bash
# list the last five charges for a workspace
acme billing charges --workspace ws_123 --limit 5

# retry the most recent failed charge
acme billing retry --workspace ws_123
```

## Read-only mode

In read-only mode users can view tickets but cannot create or reply to them. Paying the open invoice restores full access within a minute.
"
}

{
  "title": "Security policy",
  "body": "# Account security policy

## Verifying identity

Before changing anything on a customer's account, the agent must confirm that the person writing in is an owner or admin of the workspace. Confirmation means the request comes from the email address on the account, or the customer answers the security question stored in the admin panel, or the customer replies from a verified email to a code the agent sends. A matching name is not enough. A matching company domain is not enough either, because former employees often keep access to old mailboxes for weeks after they leave. If none of the three checks pass, the agent replies that the change cannot be made and explains how an existing owner can make it instead. Agents must never read out, email, or confirm any part of a stored password, recovery code, or API key, not even the last four characters. Agents must never disable two-factor authentication on request; the customer has to use a recovery code, or an existing owner has to remove and re-invite the user. If a customer claims to be locked out of every owner account in the workspace, the ticket goes to the security team with the workspace id and a short summary, and the agent tells the customer that the security team will contact them within one business day. Requests that mention legal action, law enforcement, or a court order are never handled by support; they are forwarded to the legal team unchanged and the agent does not reply with any account details. Agents who suspect an account takeover, for example a sudden change of owner email followed by a request to export all data, freeze the export and escalate to security straight away, even if the request seems to come from a verified address. Every identity check, passed or failed, is recorded as an internal note on the ticket, so that a later reviewer can see which check was used and why the change was or was not made. Agents also must not change the billing email, the workspace name, or the list of owners on the strength of a phone call, because caller id is easy to fake and calls leave no written trail. When a verified owner asks to add a new owner, the agent sends the invite to the new person's address and never shares an invite link in the ticket thread itself. If the customer pushes back on any of these checks, the agent explains that the checks protect the customer's own data, and does not make an exception, even for large accounts or urgent requests. Exceptions are only possible with written approval from the security team, and that approval is pasted into the ticket as an internal note before the change is made.

## Reporting a breach

If an agent believes customer data was exposed, they stop work on the ticket and page the on-call security engineer. They do not tell the customer anything about a possible breach until security has confirmed what happened.
"
}

{
  "title": "Api quickstart",
  "body": "This page shows how to call the Acme API from a script.

# Authentication

Every request needs an API key in the Authorization header. Create keys under Settings > API keys. A key belongs to one workspace and can be revoked at any time.

```bash
# Keys start with ak_ and are shown only once, so store yours right away.
export ACME_KEY=ak_live_example

curl https://api.acme.example/v1/me \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACME_KEY"
```

# Listing invoices

```python
# The client pages through results for you.
import acme

client = acme.Client(api_key="ak_live_example")

# Only invoices from the workspace that owns the key are returned.
for invoice in client.invoices.list(status="open"):
    print(invoice.id, invoice.amount_due)
```

The response includes at most 100 invoices per page. Pass `starting_after` with the last id to fetch the next page.

## Errors

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|--------|---------|------------|
| 401 | Missing or revoked key | Create a new key |
| 404 | Invoice is in another workspace | Check which key you used |
| 429 | Too many requests | Wait for the Retry-After seconds |

#Not a heading, because there is no space after the hash.
"
}

{
  "title": "Onboarding handbook",
  "body": "Welcome to the support team. Read this handbook in your first week; your lead will walk through it with you on day three.

# Your first week

**Day one.** You get access to the desk, the admin panel, and the team chat on your first morning. If any of the three does not work by noon, tell your lead, because the access request has to be approved by IT before the end of the day or it waits until the next weekly batch.

Spend the afternoon reading closed tickets from the last month. Pick tickets with the tags billing, login, and integrations, since those three tags make up most of the queue. Do not reply to any open tickets yet, even simple ones; customers see the name of whoever replies first, and the first reply sets their expectations for the whole conversation.

Write down every question you have while reading. Nothing is too small. Most questions new agents ask on day one are already answered in the knowledge base, and finding those answers is the fastest way to learn where things live.

At the end of the day, send your list of questions to your lead. They will mark the ones that are answered in the knowledge base so you can look them up, and answer the rest in your day two meeting.

**Day two.** On day two you shadow an experienced agent for the whole morning. Sit next to them, or join their screen share if you are remote. Watch how they read a ticket before replying: they check the customer's plan, the last three tickets from the same workspace, and any open incidents, before they type a single word.

Ask them why they chose each reply. Good agents often skip a step from the handbook on purpose, and the reason is usually more useful than the step itself. Note those reasons down; they become the edge cases you will meet later.

After lunch you draft replies to five open tickets, but you do not send them. Your shadow reviews each draft with you and either sends it as written, edits it, or explains why a different reply is better.

Finish the day by tagging twenty closed tickets that are missing tags. Tagging trains you to recognize ticket types quickly, which is what makes triage fast later.

**Day three.** Day three is your first day on the live queue, with a cap of ten tickets. Your lead reviews every reply you send that day within an hour of sending it.

Pick tickets from the top of the queue in order. Do not skip a ticket because it looks hard; flag it for your lead instead, and they will either take it or pair with you on it.

If a customer is angry, acknowledge the problem in the first sentence, say what you will do next, and give a time when they will hear back. Never promise a refund, a credit, or a fix date that is not already confirmed in the ticket or the knowledge base.

At the end of day three you and your lead review all ten tickets together. Expect most of the feedback to be about tone and about asking for missing information up front, rather than about product knowledge.

# Escalation

Escalate a ticket when it needs someone with more access, more authority, or more product knowledge than you have. Escalating early is always better than guessing.

Use the Escalate button, not a chat message. The button records who escalated, when, and why, and the ticket keeps its place in the queue's response time reporting.
"
}
